content: Google DeepMind ships Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash with 4K video and scene extension — AI Chat Daily ... Google DeepMind ships Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash with 4K video and scene extension ... The Omni update pushes generative video to 4K, extends clips to 40 seconds, and cuts draft costs to a third at 360p. ... Google DeepMind released Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash today, a production-ready update to its generative video model that adds 4K upscaling, scene extension up to 40 seconds, and first-and-last-frame interpolation. The model is live through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Adobe, Figma, and GMI Cloud are already shipping it inside production tools. The update is aimed squarely at developers building video workflows, not at consumer prompt-and-pray toys. ... The headline additions are control features that generative video has been missing. Scene extension now works in 10-second increments up to a cumulative 40 seconds, with the model analyzing 10 seconds of prior context to keep characters, lighting, and camera motion consistent. That is a step change from earlier Omni releases, which referenced only the final second of a clip before generating what came next. ... . Google Deep ... - 01Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash extends generated scenes up to a cumulative 40 seconds, in 10-second increments. - 02The model can now reason over 10 seconds of prior context, up from the final second in earlier versions. - 03360p drafts generate up to faster and cost a third of standard 720p output. - 04Final output can be upscaled to 1080p or 4K, with video references up to three seconds long. - 05Adobe Firefly, Figma Weave, and GMI Cloud are already shipping the model in production. ... The economics matter as much as the controls. Omni 1.1 Flash can generate 360p previews up to faster than 720p output and at roughly a third of the cost, which turns iteration from an expensive gamble into cheap scouting. Once a draft is approved, the same model upscales to 1080p or 4K for finishing. That two-tier pattern — cheap drafts, expensive finals — has been standard in film pipelines for decades, and Google DeepMind is finally bringing it to generative video. ... Adobe has integrated the model into Firefly for video editing, and Figma Weave is using it as one of the core generators on its canvas. GMI Cloud is running it through the Agent Platform API for production customers. Product managers Anish Nangia and Alisa Fortin, who authored the announcement, framed the release as the point at which Omni crosses from demo to deployment.

content: Aug 29, 2026 94 approx.9min News Factory Verified Alibaba's Qwen team has released and open-sourced Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125B-parameter multimodal MoE model with only 6B active parameters per token, priced at approximately of Claude Opus4.6 with training costs reduced by about . Its "Next" architecture is positioned as the technical prototype for the upcoming Qwen4 flagship. On the evening of August 26, 2026, Alibaba's Qwen team officially released and open-sourced Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 125B Transformer parameters and only 6B activated per token. Training costs are approximately lower than the previous-generation Qwen3.7-Plus. API pricing is set at 1 RMB per million input tokens and 3 RMB per million output tokens, which the company states is roughly of Claude Opus4.6's pricing. The complete model weights have been simultaneously published on Hugging Face and the ModelScope community for direct download by developers worldwide. ... Based on benchmark data released officially and compiled by independent media outlet DataCamp, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next shows clear advantages in agentic programming and professional office tasks. On the SWE-bench Pro programming benchmark, the model scores 62.5 versus Claude Opus4.6's 53.4, a gap of 9.1 points; on CoWorkBench for long-horizon professional tasks, it leads 73.9 to 68.2; on JobBench for professional work tasks, the gap widens to 55.7 versus 36.6, a roughly 19-point margin. In the multimodal dimension, it leads Opus4.6 by 22.5 points on AndroidWorld for mobile agent tasks, 25.1 points on MathVision for visual math reasoning, and 31.5 points on the ERQA embodied intelligence task. ... But this report card is not a one-sided rout. According to DataCamp, on Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a comprehensive reasoning challenge, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next scores 35.9, below Claude Opus4.6's 40.0. HLE is designed to test models' reasoning ability near the boundaries of knowledge, and the score gap indicates that Qwen3.8-Flash-Next still lags behind leading closed-source models in extreme reasoning depth. Its strengths are more concentrated in engineering-oriented tasks and multimodal scenarios rather than general intellectual reasoning. ... title: Google DeepMind Ran History's First AI Benchmark Evaluation Where Neither Side Could Cheat
summary: Google DeepMind Ran History's First AI Benchmark Evaluation Where Neither Side Could Cheat Deepmind.google For years, the AI evaluation industry had one structural problem no contractual safeguard could solve: whoever runs the test either has to hand the model provider the questions, or hand the e
content: Google DeepMind Ran History's First AI Benchmark Evaluation Where Neither Side Could Cheat ... For years, the AI evaluation industry had one structural problem no contractual safeguard could solve: whoever runs the test either has to hand the model provider the questions, or hand the evaluator the model. On August 27, 2026, Google DeepMind announced the world's first double-blind evaluation of a proprietary frontier-class AI model — one that required neither compromise, using cryptographic hardware to seal Gemini's weights and an external evaluator's benchmark prompts simultaneously inside a single hardware-encrypted enclave where neither party could see the other's protected data. ... The pilot, conducted in partnership with Singapore's AI Safety Institute (AISI), privacy-computing nonprofit OpenMined, AI benchmarking consortium MLCommons, and evaluation firm AVERI, tested Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite against confidential benchmarks — and its significance has nothing to do with how Gemini scored. What matters is how the test was run: for the first time in the industry's history, a model provider and an independent evaluator conducted a formal evaluation without either side needing to trust the other's word about what data they had seen. ... The most consequential ... For now, the pilot stands as the first production-level proof that the adversarial trust problem at the center of AI benchmarking can be made architecturally irrelevant — not by improving procedures, but by removing the attack surface those procedures were trying to protect. ... Not automatically, and not universally. This pilot addresses one specific failure mode — the ability of a model provider to see evaluation prompts before or during a test, and the reciprocal risk of an evaluator seeing proprietary model weights. It does not address benchmark quality, benchmark management after the evaluation, or the question of whether the benchmark itself is well-designed and resistant to other forms of gaming. MLCommons explicitly noted that benchmark quality still requires careful management regardless of how well the prompts are protected during evaluation. And the pilot is currently limited to models that fit on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, which excludes the largest frontier systems. What this pilot does provide is a mechanism: for the first time, an independent organization can evaluate a proprietary model against confidential benchmarks and produce results that neither side could have seen in advance — which is the necessary precondition for trustworthy evaluation, even if it is not sufficient on its own.
